Question: What are the safest seats on an airplane?
Answer: It really depends on the accident. In one crash the guys in front are killed, and in another, the guys in the back are killed. Rule-of-thumb, the back of the airplane is usually the safest. Japan Airlines Flight 123 impacted mountains at high-speed after the Boeing 747 lost a huge piece of the tail. The four survivors were all seated in the last few rows of the 747. When American Airlines Flight 965 flew head-first into the mountain, the survivors were seated in the back of the 757. But an accident where the back is not the safest is in a water-landing. A water landing calls for the airplane to impact tail-first, thus sacrificing everybody in the tail section. When the airplane hits the water, because you land without landing gear in the water, the back of the airplane will likely break off, killing everyone here. The guys in the front will survive if they don't drown. When an airplane catches fire, it's really a toss of the dice. Depending where the fire is coming from, it's probably best to sit far away from the fire. But in the event of a fire, you only have about 22 minutes to go from cruise to landing, so it won't really matter where you sit anyways. If the airplane explodes due to a fuel fire, it's best to sit away from the wings, where the fuel is stored. There are so many variables in determining the safest seat on an aeroplane. It really depends on the emergency and the crash.

Question: Why do airplanes only fly at 39000 feet and not higher?
Answer: Airplanes can fly way above 39,000 feet. In fact, the Citation X I flew on today cruised at 45,000 feet. Some airplanes at certain weights may be limited to cruising altitudes at or below 39,000 feet. This is because heavier airplanes in general require more lift due to the extra weight they may be carrying. Because air is thinner at higher altitudes, something like a Boeing 747 at MTOW may only be able to make 33 or 34,000 feet, simply because it is so heavy. But once the aircraft burns off enough fuel, it can fly easily above 39,000 feet. Most transport jets can make FL 390 or more if light enough.

Due to a slight over-estimation of Neptune’s mass, peculiarities in Uranus’s orbit were perceived to be caused by an extra giant planet, leading to an intense search and ultimately the discovery of Pluto.
